801.quote_or_event: Bhai Mardana, a Muslim minstrel of Guru Nanak's own village and ten years older than him, went to Sultanpur and, in the words of the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, never parted company with Guru Nanak again; he played the rabab as the Guru sang through all his long journeys until his death at Kartarpur in 1534.
801.explanation: Mardana is the classic Sikh example of a lifelong companion: a friend from childhood who stayed with Guru Nanak across decades of travel and hardship.
801.tie_back: The Kural defines old friendship as a bond that has grown through long closeness and bears the freedoms that time brings; the decades-long companionship of Guru Nanak and Mardana is the Sikh tradition's picture of such a friendship.
801.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh (paraphrase)
801._accuracy_note: A fitting example of long-standing companionship, but the relationship was also that of disciple and Guru, and many details rest on the Janamsakhi tradition rather than on contemporary records.

802.quote_or_event: According to the Puratan Janamsakhi, soon after leaving Sultanpur Mardana complained of hunger, went to a nearby village on the Guru's suggestion, and came back loaded with a bundle of gifts; Guru Nanak rolled on the ground laughing, and Mardana, seeing the oddity of what he had done, threw the bundle away.
802.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism notes that the biographers tell several such humorous stories of Mardana's amiable faux pas, which the Guru met with laughter and patience rather than reproach.
802.tie_back: The Kural says the freedoms friends take are part of friendship and the good should welcome and relish them; Guru Nanak's laughter at Mardana's blunder shows that kind of easy, affectionate tolerance between old companions.
802.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh, citing the Puratan Janamsakhi (paraphrase)
802._accuracy_note: According to the Janamsakhi tradition, which is hagiography; it shows affectionate tolerance of a friend's lapses, but the episode's own point is that possessions are a burden, not the ethics of intimate liberty.

803.quote_or_event: “My Guru is always with me, near at hand. … Your actions seem so sweet to me.”
803.explanation: In this Aasaa shabad Guru Arjan speaks of the Guru as an ever-present companion and says that whatever the Beloved does is sweet to him.
803.tie_back: The Kural asks what use long friendship is if one will not accept what the friend does by right of closeness as though one had done it oneself; Guru Arjan's line shows that attitude of owning and welcoming whatever the closest companion does.
803.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 394, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
803._accuracy_note: Next-best match: the attitude of accepting a beloved's acts as sweet is close, but Guru Arjan addresses God and the Guru, not a human friend, and nothing here speaks of long acquaintance.

804.quote_or_event: When Mardana lay dying at Kartarpur in 1534, Guru Nanak asked how he wished his body to be disposed of; Mardana replied that by the Guru's teaching he had overcome pride in the body, and whatever remained should be disposed of as the Guru wished. He declined a tomb, and the Guru consigned his body to the River Ravi.
804.explanation: Mardana left the most personal decision of all to his old companion without asking for anything, trusting that whatever Guru Nanak chose would be right.
804.tie_back: The Kural says the wise welcome what a close friend does for them unasked, as though they had wanted it; Mardana's leaving his own last rites to Guru Nanak shows that complete trust in an old friend's choices.
804.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Mardana, Bhai (1459-1534)' by Satbir Singh (paraphrase)
804._accuracy_note: Shows trust in a lifelong companion's decisions, but the decision was invited rather than taken unasked, and the relationship is also that of disciple and Guru; the account derives from the Janamsakhi tradition.

805.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
805.explanation: Kabir ranks forgiveness (khima) as the highest of the virtues he lists, the place where God Himself is present.
805.tie_back: The Kural tells us to excuse a friend's hurtful act as ignorance or the freedom of great intimacy; Kabir's salok gives the Sikh ground for that charity, since forgiveness is where God dwells.
805.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
805._accuracy_note: Supports the forgiving disposition the Kural asks for, but is a general teaching on forgiveness and does not offer the Kural's two specific explanations (ignorance or intimacy) for a friend's offence.

806.quote_or_event: “Kabir! If the mortal continues to love the Lord in the end, as he pledged in the beginning, no poor diamond, not even millions of jewels, can equal him.”
806.explanation: Kabir praises love that stays the same at the end as it was at the beginning, and says such constancy is worth more than any treasure.
806.tie_back: The Kural says those who keep to the true bounds of friendship never give up long-standing friends even when it costs them; Kabir prizes the same constancy of a love kept to the end as it was pledged.
806.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 153 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
806._accuracy_note: A good fit on unchanging, lifelong loyalty, but Kabir speaks of love for God, not for an old human friend, and does not mention loss or harm.

807.quote_or_event: “Farid, answer evil with goodness; do not fill your mind with anger. Your body shall not suffer from any disease, and you shall obtain everything.”
807.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib, counsels returning good for harm and refusing to let anger take root in the mind.
807.tie_back: The Kural says those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving even when their friends bring them ruin; Farid's counsel to answer evil with goodness is the disposition that makes such love possible.
807.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381-1382, Salok Sheikh Farid 78 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
807._accuracy_note: A reasonable parallel on unbroken goodwill toward those who harm us, though Farid speaks of anyone who does evil, not specifically of old friends.

808.quote_or_event: “Farid, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
808.explanation: Farid tells the wise not to keep a record of other people's faults but to examine their own.
808.tie_back: The Kural praises the person so secure in friendship that he will not even listen to talk of his friend's faults; Farid's refusal to write black marks against others is the same refusal to dwell on a companion's failings.
808.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
808._accuracy_note: Matches the refusal to dwell on others' faults, but it is general self-examination rather than trust in a particular friend, and it does not touch the Kural's paradox that the friend's lapse becomes a day of gain.

809.quote_or_event: Bhai (later Baba) Buddha met Guru Nanak as a boy and served the Gurus for the rest of a very long life: he applied the tilak at the installation of Guru Angad and of the four Gurus after him, helped dig the tank at Amritsar, became the first granthi of the Harimandar in 1604, and trained the young Hargobind. When he died in 1631, Guru Hargobind was at his bedside and gave his shoulder to the bier.
809.explanation: Baba Buddha's unbroken loyalty across six Gurus made him one of the most venerated figures of early Sikhism, honoured by the Guru himself at his death.
809.tie_back: The Kural says the world loves those who never let go of friendships handed down through the years; Baba Buddha, who kept faith with the Gurus' house for over a century, is remembered with exactly that love and honour.
809.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Buddha, Baba (1506-1631)' by Gurdip Singh Randhawa (paraphrase)
809._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of lifelong loyalty earning esteem, though it is devotion to the Gurus rather than friendship between equals; some details rest on later sources such as the Gurbilas.

810.quote_or_event: “Farid, do not turn around and strike those who strike you with their fists. Kiss their feet, and return to your own home.”
810.explanation: Farid counsels meeting hostility with humility instead of retaliation.
810.tie_back: The Kural says those who never fall from goodwill toward old friends, even when the friends err, are loved even by those who wish them ill; Farid's refusal to strike back is the kind of steady goodwill that can disarm ill-wishers.
810.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 7 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
810._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it shares the ethic of unbroken goodwill under provocation, but says nothing about old friends or about enemies coming to love such a person.
